profile.name: Yasin Billah
profile.tagline: I take software products from kickoff to launch and own everything in between — scope, sprints, QA, and release. 6 shipped in the last 11 months for clients in Korea, Japan, the US, and Europe.

highlights.label: Faster delivery after going AI-native (3 months → 1)

story.statementLead: Most projects do not fail on the plan. They fail in the gap between
story.statementEm: what a client asked for and what a developer heard
story.statementTail: — and closing that gap, every day, is the job.
paragraphs: Four years in the software industry — I started as a front-end developer, moved through QA, and have spent the last three running delivery. That path is why the gap is narrower on my projects: I read the code, so I can argue scope with an engineer instead of relaying messages, and I ran QA, so I know which "small change" is actually small.

The other half of the job is people. A stalled sprint is rarely a planning problem — it is a developer who is blocked and has not said so, or a client whose real objection has not surfaced yet. I get both into the open early, give the team cover to work, and take the difficult conversation myself rather than passing it down.

I have shipped marketplaces, mobile-AI apps, ERP, and SaaS for clients across Japan, Korea, the US, and the EU. The AI-native workflows I build in Claude Code, n8n, and Notion cut average client delivery from three months to one — with the same ceremonies, documentation, and QA pass still in place.

howIOperate.title: The hard conversation is mine
howIOperate.body: When a date is going to slip or a request is out of scope, the client hears it from me — early, with options. Bad news travels badly when it is delegated, and a client who finds out late stops trusting the next update.

howIOperate.title: Cover for the team
howIOperate.body: Developers do their best work when they are not fielding status questions. I absorb the reporting, unblock quietly, and make sure a stuck engineer can say so without it costing them anything.

howIOperate.title: AI as leverage, not as an excuse
howIOperate.body: The workflows I build in Claude Code, n8n, and Notion cut average client delivery from three months to one — with standups, reviews, retrospectives, and the SQA pass all still in place.

howIOperate.title: PM and QA, same person
howIOperate.body: I write the test cases and run the SQA pass myself. Owning both the schedule and the quality bar means I cannot quietly trade one for the other.

pmProcess.title: Kickoff & scoping
pmProcess.caption: Turn the ask into a plan
pmProcess.body: I start at pre-sale kickoff: learn the client’s business and what they are actually trying to achieve, then translate that into a deliverable-oriented WBS with man-hour estimation, resource and budget plans, and a risk assessment — before development starts. Scoping the budget and tech stack this early is what keeps delivery off a guess.

pmProcess.title: Plan & setup
pmProcess.caption: Make the plan visible
pmProcess.body: Communication strategy, sprint plan, and one source of truth everyone works from. At Potential I architected the company’s end-to-end Agile/Scrum delivery system in Notion, so every project runs the same way from kickoff through to closure rather than depending on who is running it.

pmProcess.title: Execution & control
pmProcess.caption: Hold the line day to day
pmProcess.body: Daily standups in Notion and the PM Dashboard ticket system, variance analysis against the plan, and escalation while there is still time to act. Change goes through change control with stakeholder buy-in, never by drift. The AI workflows I build in Claude Code and n8n are what cut average client delivery from three months to one.

pmProcess.title: QA, UAT & release
pmProcess.caption: Own the quality bar, not just the date
pmProcess.body: I run QA and UAT hands-on rather than handing the quality bar to someone else — it comes from starting in QA. Then app-store submission and release management through to launch, so "shipped" means live in front of users, not merged.

capabilities.intro: I pair project leadership with the technical depth to ship, not just spec. Four years turning ambiguous requirements into launched products across marketplaces, EdTech, ERP, mobile-AI, and HR-tech.

contribution: Delivered in two phases: Phase 1 took the platform to an MVP where every order was functional end-to-end; Phase 2 added role-based access, multiple payment terms, and multi-office support.
Ran the project from kickoff: requirement gathering, user stories, PRD and SRS, technical decisions, and design requirements and guidelines.
Owned the design loop — wrote the UI/UX direction, reviewed and fed back on screens, and signed off before build.
Ran Agile/Scrum to the letter: daily standups, sprint planning, sprint review, and retrospectives, with weekly client meetings and daily written updates.

livePreview.alt: Ivorymade order detail with order information, tracking, and order actions

sections.title: Phase 1 - every order functional
sections.body: Phase 1 was a genuine MVP, not a demo: a case could be submitted, designed, reviewed against the 3D model, produced, and invoiced without leaving the platform. Anything not required to make an order work was deliberately deferred.
sections.quote: Make the order the unit of truth before adding who is allowed to do what.

image.alt: Ivorymade order detail screen showing order information, tracking, and order actions
image.caption: Order detail - submission, tracking, and actions in one place.

sections.title: Phase 2 - roles, terms, offices
sections.body: Once the order flow was stable, the platform grew into how labs are actually structured: role-based access so technicians, reviewers, and administrators see different things; multiple payment terms rather than one billing assumption; and multi-office support for groups running several locations.

sections.title: 3D model review
sections.body: Restoration review runs on the exocad viewer inside the platform, so the technician and the reviewing dentist look at the same model rather than exchanging files.

image.alt: Ivorymade 3D design model review using the embedded exocad viewer
image.caption: 3D design model review - exocad viewer embedded in the order flow.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Art appraisal is a trust transaction before it is a commercial one. A collector needs to believe the expert is qualified; the expert needs to be paid without chasing invoices. Get either half wrong and there is no second attempt.

image.alt: Artlive landing experience - connect with certified art experts and choose a service
image.caption: Discovery leads with certified experts and a clear service choice.

sections.title: Model the money first
sections.body: Payments were the constraint everything else had to fit, so the architecture was settled before feature work began. Stripe Connect splits platform and expert; PayPal covers collectors who will not use anything else. Deciding this at specification time kept three service flows from becoming three payment implementations.
sections.quote: Three service flows, one payment model - decided before the first sprint.

image.alt: Artlive expert profile showing online valuation, buyer support, and bespoke service pricing
image.caption: Each service carries its own scope, turnaround, and price shape.

sections.title: Make expertise legible
sections.body: Discovery leads with credentials, specialisms, and previously reviewed objects, because in this market the expert profile is the product. That shaped the design guidelines I wrote for the team.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Standing in front of a piece of art, the information you want is immediate and the patience you have is short. A placard gives you a title; a search engine gives you fifty results for the wrong painting. The gap is recognition.

image.alt: Bside mobile app home screen showing the artwork feed
image.caption: The app opens on the feed - recognition is one tap away.

sections.title: Recognition as a separate service
sections.body: The mobile client and the PyTorch recognition pipeline were built as separate services, with the model served from AWS ECS. Recognition could iterate on its own cadence without blocking the app, and the client stayed thin enough to ship to two stores on schedule.
sections.quote: A pipeline that is accurate but slow fails the moment of use as completely as one that is fast and wrong.

image.alt: Bside artwork detail view with the recognised work and artist context
image.caption: Recognition result - the work, the artist, and the context.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Collectible marketplaces live or die on whether a listing represents the item accurately and whether both sides trust the transaction. Trading cards make both harder, because condition is the price - the same card in two grades is effectively two different products.

image.alt: Cart Traders mobile app showing the trading-card marketplace feed
image.caption: Discovery has to make condition and price legible at a glance.

sections.title: Listing flow above everything
sections.body: In a two-sided market the supply side is the bottleneck at launch, so I specified the listing path as the highest-priority experience: fewest steps, camera-first, and condition captured as structured data rather than free text.
sections.quote: Free-text condition notes are unsearchable and unenforceable. Grade had to be a field.

image.alt: Cart Traders listing flow capturing card details and condition
image.caption: Structured condition capture, so discovery and pricing share one source.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Sports-ticket supply is fast and high-variance: inventory changes value by the hour, every supplier has its own terms, and a mistake is immediately visible to a customer holding a ticket that does not work. Operations teams run on spreadsheets plus relationships until volume makes that untenable.
sections.quote: The failure mode is not dramatic - it is small reconciliation errors nobody has time to chase.

image.alt: Trustix dashboard overview showing supplier and inventory state
image.caption: Supplier state made observable rather than remembered.

sections.title: Start from the operator day
sections.body: For an internal tool the specification that matters is the sequence a person actually performs between opening the dashboard and closing it. I wrote the user stories from that sequence, which kept the build focused on reducing clicks in high-frequency paths rather than covering every theoretical case.

image.alt: Trustix supplier detail view with terms and fulfilment history
image.caption: The high-frequency paths got the design attention.

sections.title: Supplier terms as data
sections.body: Each supplier has different arrangements. Encoding those as configuration rather than special-case logic was the technical decision with the longest tail - it determines whether adding a supplier later is a form entry or a development ticket.

image.alt: Trustix supplier configuration screen showing per-supplier terms
image.caption: Adding a supplier is a form entry, not a release.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Discovery apps in the experiences space tend to optimise for inventory breadth and leave the user to filter. The result is a catalogue, and a catalogue puts the work back on the person who came looking for a recommendation.

sections.title: Budget the onboarding
sections.body: Every question asked before a user sees value is a chance to lose them. I specified onboarding as a fixed budget of interactions rather than an open list of preferences to collect, which forced the team to decide which signals genuinely improved matching.
sections.quote: Personalisation needs signal before the user has given you much. That is the design problem.

sections.title: Kickoff & scoping
sections.body: Requirement gathering, user stories, PRD and SRS, technical decisions, and the design requirements and guidelines — all before development started. Scoping the budget and stack this early is what keeps delivery off a guess.

sections.title: Design direction
sections.body: I wrote the UI/UX direction rather than waiting for screens to review, then ran the feedback loop with the designers and signed off before build. Owning the design brief is what keeps revision cycles short.

sections.title: Delivery process
sections.body: Agile/Scrum run properly: daily standups, sprint planning, sprint review, and retrospectives, with weekly client meetings and a written update every day. The cadence is the product — it is what makes status a fact instead of an opinion.

sections.title: Quality & SQA
sections.body: I wrote the test cases and ran the SQA pass myself rather than handing the quality bar to someone else. That comes from starting in QA, and it means I find the problems before the client does.

sections.title: A product you cannot count
sections.body: Generic ERP breaks on apparel because a product is not a countable thing. "Polo shirt for men" is an article; what a warehouse holds is that article multiplied by colour and size — often thirty or more items. Childrenswear is worse, because sizes are age bands from Newborn to 11–12 years.
sections.quote: Count articles instead of items and every number downstream is quietly wrong.

image.alt: Jintech Business Suite platform overview showing its integrated modules
image.caption: Four systems that have to agree: ordering, inventory, accounting, POS.

sections.title: Stock lives in a network
sections.body: A dispatching unit, a receiving store, a main warehouse, a retail warehouse and regional godowns. The same item sits in several places at once, so "stock" is meaningless without asking where — and transfers between them change availability without touching the ledger.

sections.title: What low-code actually buys
sections.body: Claris FileMaker lets the client edit and build their own reports without a developer — which deletes a whole category of change request for a business whose reporting shifts every season. The cost is the platform ceiling: its interface conventions, its licensing, and a much smaller pool of engineers. That last one is a resourcing risk, not a technical one.
sections.quote: Low-code moved the constraint. It did not remove it.

sections.title: Permissions as a feature
sections.body: More than ten privilege sets: data-entry only, read-only, report-print users, finance groups split by which accounts they may touch, and a closed-accounting-year group that can read a locked period but not post into it. Where the person entering stock must not be the person adjusting the ledger, access control is the product, not configuration.

sections.title: Specifying for a room you are not in
sections.body: Requirements arrived through Japanese stakeholders for Pakistani and Bangladeshi operations, with demos subtitled in Japanese. The person approving a requirement was often not the person who discussed it, which raises the bar on written specification: a PRD that only reminds you of a conversation is useless to someone who was never in it.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Testing an ad campaign means spending money to find out it does not work. The feedback loop is expensive, slow, and only tells you the result - not which part of the creative caused it. Brand-AId simulates the campaign against a synthetic market first.
sections.quote: Not to replace measurement - to catch the campaigns that were obviously going to underperform.

sections.title: A pipeline, not a prompt
sections.body: Seven distinct stages: campaign analysis, audience research, persona generation, forecasting, recommendations, re-simulation, and a QA review. Separating them makes each stage independently inspectable, which is what makes the output arguable rather than a black box.

sections.title: Ground the numbers
sections.body: A forecast produced entirely by a language model is a guess with good grammar. The forecast engine uses a Random Forest trained on a real dataset to anchor click-through and return-on-spend, with RAG retrieval pulling benchmarks from a knowledge base. The LLM explains and recommends; the model predicts.

sections.title: Audit the AI with AI
sections.body: The final stage is an independent LLM review with function calling, checking the pipeline’s own output for arithmetic errors and internal contradictions. Building a QA step into the product came straight from running SQA on client projects.

sections.title: One week, solo
sections.body: Product decisions and code, both mine, start to finish in a week. That scope is not a one-week scope on a legacy workflow - it is what the AI-native approach looks like with no team as a variable.
sections.quote: The strongest answer I have to "can you actually build, or do you just manage people who do".

projects.name: TakaPay Pulse
projects.solution: Social-Listening Dashboard with an AI Assistant
projects.summary: A social-listening dashboard that turns 660 raw posts into what a brand manager should do next — an auditable cleaning pipeline, a bilingual sentiment audit, and an assistant whose numbers are computed by code, not estimated by a model.
contribution: Built the product and the code solo, end to end.
Designed an ingestion pipeline where nothing reaches the UI unaudited.
Shipped an AI assistant that answers with computed figures rather than generated ones.

livePreview.alt: TakaPay Pulse dashboard showing sentiment breakdown and topic analysis

sections.title: The real question
sections.body: A brand manager does not ask "what is the sentiment" — they ask "what do I do today". So the headline panel ranks issues by negative volume weighted by the attention each post draws, with a plain-language action per issue. In this data the answer was loud: failed transactions, 215 posts, 100% negative after the audit, and the most engaged theme on the feed.
sections.quote: Sentiment is a number. "Fix this first" is a product.

image.alt: TakaPay Pulse dashboard with the what-needs-attention panel and sentiment charts
image.caption: The dashboard leads with the decision, not the chart.

sections.title: Nothing renders unaudited
sections.body: Every record passes sources → validate → normalize → dedupe → relevance → sentiment audit before the UI sees it. The API returns the cleaned data plus a full quality report: every excluded or corrected record with its evidence. Nothing is changed silently — corrected posts carry a visible marker.

sections.title: The bilingual catch
sections.body: My first cleaning pass was English-only and looked fine. Reviewing the posts table showed Bangla complaints still labeled positive — "still hasn't arrived" scored 91. The English-only rules caught 22 mislabels and silently missed 15, and those 15 were exactly the Bangla-script records. Extending the audit took corrections from 22 to 37.
sections.quote: An English-first pass on Bangladeshi social data silently under-counts the negative.

sections.title: The assistant computes, it does not guess
sections.body: "Ask Pulse" turns plain-language questions into tool calls over the cleaned data, so every number in an answer is calculated by code — a language model never estimates a figure. Answers show which filters produced them, and one click applies those filters to the dashboard.

image.alt: TakaPay Pulse analysis views including topic sentiment split and engagement breakdown
image.caption: Every figure on screen traces back to a record in the posts table.

sections.title: Where I overrode the AI
sections.body: I used Claude Code heavily and the decisions stayed mine. I rejected two drafts of the topics panel that drew every topic the same width, so a 2-post topic looked as large as a 215-post one. When the engagement analysis came back flat, I shipped the flatness as the finding rather than four empty comparisons — flat engagement plus templated wording points at manufactured volume. And a rising negative share is red regardless of which way the arrow points, against the dashboard convention of colouring "up" green.
sections.quote: The data overruled the template.

sections.title: AI checking AI
sections.body: A scripted browser sweep of 29 checks — filters, search, date comparison maths, pagination, click-throughs, and the assistant returning real computed numbers — ran before ship. It caught a deploy-breaking detail (the chat route needs its model key present at build time) before it reached the live demo.
